To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the adoption of a CPOE system in the hospital setting engendered workarounds that were created by clinicians to compensate for the system's limitations and the changing nature and complexity of the clinical work environment.

1) the CPOE system was used as an assemblage of objects, including the CPOE software, the computer, and the paper prescription pad; 2) the CPOEs assemblage was a boundary object that enabled clinicians to work around the system, but the CPOE assemblage also changed clinical practice, which in turn led to the development of new assemblages that were also used as boundary objects to work around the CPOE; 3

the adoption of a CPOE system in a teaching hospital has resulted in the creation of workarounds, and these workarounds are a manifestation of the changing clinical practices that are now more computerized.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how clinicians work around CPOE systems and how these workarounds may be understood as boundary objects that mediate between the clinical and the technological.
the interplay between technology and work practice, and how the two are shaped by each other in the process of technology adoption.
how clinicians work around the CPOE system, how the workarounds change, and how the changes are related to the CPOE adoption.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
workarounds, assemblages, and boundary objects are all interrelated and are all important to understand the changes of work practices in a hospital environment.

workarounds are not only the result of a system's failure to meet the needs of users, but also a way to accommodate the changes brought by a new system and to maintain the continuity of the clinical work.

the adoption of a CPOE system in a large teaching hospital has resulted in a number of changes to medical practice, including changes in how doctors and nurses order medications and how they communicate with each other.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

clinicians' workarounding behavior is an important aspect of clinical practice and should be studied in order to understand how clinical practice is changing in the face of the increasing adoption of computerized clinical information systems.
clinicians' workarrounds are not only a way to adapt to the CPOE system, but also a way to adapt their work practices to the changing nature of the work environment.
CPOE systems are not simply tools for clinicians to work with, but rather, they are a part of the work environment and are embedded in the work practices of clinicians.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the CPOE system has changed clinical practice in ways that are not necessarily visible to the users.
the concept of boundary object, as originally defined by Star and Griesemer (1989), may be insufficient to explain the workarounds that we observed.
the adoption of CPOE systems is a complex and dynamic process, with workarounds being one of the many manifestations of the process.
